body.en: A series \( \sum a_n \) converges when its partial sums \( S_N=\sum_{n=1}^{N}a_n \) approach a finite limit. Since we rarely sum infinitely many terms by hand, a battery of tests decides convergence from the shape of \( a_n \) alone.

If \( \displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n\neq 0 \), then \( \sum a_n \) diverges. Caution: \( a_n\to 0 \) does not guarantee convergence — the harmonic series \( \sum \tfrac1n \) diverges even though its terms vanish.

The p-series \( \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^{p}} \) converges if and only if \( p\gt 1 \). For positive terms, if \( 0\le a_n\le b_n \) and \( \sum b_n \) converges, so does \( \sum a_n \) (and the contrapositive for divergence).

body.en: For series with factorials or exponentials, compare a term to the one before it. Let \( \displaystyle L=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| \). Then the series converges absolutely if \( L\lt 1 \), diverges if \( L\gt 1 \), and the test is inconclusive if \( L=1 \).

label.en: ▲ Theorem 11.3 — Power series & radius of convergence

body.en: A power series \( \displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n(x-a)^{n} \) converges for all \( x \) with \( |x-a|\lt R \) and diverges for \( |x-a|\gt R \), where \( R \) is the radius of convergence. The endpoints \( x=a\pm R \) must be tested separately.

Test \( \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{n}{2^{n}} \) for convergence.

Form the ratio of successive terms and take the limit:

\[ L=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n+1}{2^{n+1}}\cdot\frac{2^{n}}{n}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n+1}{2n}=\frac12\lt 1, \]

so the series converges absolutely.

Find the radius of convergence of \( \displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^{n}}{n!} \).

The ratio of terms is \( \left|\dfrac{x^{n+1}/(n+1)!}{x^{n}/n!}\right|=\dfrac{|x|}{n+1}\to 0 \) for every \( x \). Since \( L=0\lt 1 \) always, \( R=\infty \) — this series (which is \( e^{x} \)) converges everywhere.

caption.en: Bar chart comparing term values \(a_n = \frac{n}{2^n}\) for \(n = 1, \dots, 6\), displaying rapid geometric decay toward 0 that drives convergence.

body.en:
Ratio Test Inconclusiveness (L = 1): If \(L = \lim_{n\to\infty} \left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| = 1\), the Ratio Test gives NO conclusion whatsoever. In particular, the Ratio Test ALWAYS gives \(L = 1\) for any p-series or rational fraction in \(n\); use the Comparison Test or Integral Test instead!

Testing Endpoints for Interval of Convergence: Finding the radius of convergence \(R\) determines an open interval \((a - R, a + R)\). You MUST test each endpoint \(x = a - R\) and \(x = a + R\) separately, as convergence at boundaries varies (e.g. one end might be conditionally convergent via Alternating Series while the other diverges).

Absolute vs Conditional Convergence: A series \(\sum a_n\) is conditionally convergent if \(\sum a_n\) converges, but \(\sum |a_n|\) diverges (classic example: \(\sum \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}\)).

question.en: Find the radius of convergence \(R\) of the power series \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(x - 3)^n}{n \cdot 5^n}\).

solution.en:
Apply the Ratio Test with \(a_n = \frac{(x - 3)^n}{n \cdot 5^n}\):
\[ L = \lim_{n\to\infty} \left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| = \lim_{n\to\infty} \left|\frac{(x - 3)^{n+1}}{(n+1)5^{n+1}} \cdot \frac{n \cdot 5^n}{(x - 3)^n}\right| = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{n}{n+1} \cdot \frac{|x - 3|}{5} = \frac{|x - 3|}{5}. \]
For absolute convergence, require \(L < 1 \implies \frac{|x - 3|}{5} < 1 \implies |x - 3| < 5\). Thus the radius of convergence is \(R = 5\).
